big: Rohan earns dirhams in Dubai and sends money home. Back in India, he also earns rent from a flat. If he puts both in one account, he mixes money that can go back abroad with money that can't easily.

lines: Which account do I use for what?
NRE for money you earn abroad. NRO for income earned in India. FCNR(B) for a deposit held in a foreign currency. Mixing them causes tax and transfer trouble later.

rows: Rupees from foreign earnings. Fully repatriable. Interest generally tax-exempt
Rupees for Indian income. Interest taxable. Repatriation capped
A deposit in a foreign currency, with no exchange-rate risk on principal
note: Rules change, so check the current rule with your bank or a qualified adviser.

q: Rohan gets monthly rent on his flat in India. Which account suits it?
why: NRE is meant for money earned abroad.
FCNR(B) is a foreign currency deposit, not for rent.
Income earned in India belongs in an NRO account.
He is an NRI, so a resident account is not right.

q: Meena wants her foreign savings in India to be easy to send back later. Which account fits?
opts: A joint account with a resident
why: NRE balances and interest are freely repatriable.
NRO money is capped on repatriation.
A resident account is not for NRI foreign earnings.
A joint resident account does not make money repatriable.

q: Which deposit shields Rohan's principal from rupee moves?
why: An NRO deposit is in rupees, so it is exposed to rupee moves.
A rupee savings account is exposed to rupee moves.
A rupee bond carries rupee exposure as well.
FCNR(B) is held in a foreign currency, so it avoids rupee risk.

opts: Moving money between two banks within India

Paying income tax on earnings in India
Opening a new bank account in a foreign land
why: Moving money within India is only an ordinary bank transfer.
It is sending money from India back to where you live.
Paying tax is a separate duty and not repatriation.
Opening an account is a step before any money moves.

pts: NRE for foreign earnings, NRO for Indian income.
